opus-5.5.text:
Sure. I'd actually push back a little on the word "attack," because one of the points we wanted to make is that you don't need a sophisticated adversary for things to go wrong.

A lot of prior work on RAG safety assumes a threat model where someone poisons the corpus. They plant malicious documents or inject instructions into retrieved passages and see whether the model follows them. That's a real concern, but we asked a simpler question: if you take a model that's been safety-tuned and behaves well on its own, and you just put it in a standard retrieval pipeline, does it stay safe?

So the setup is fairly vanilla. We take a set of harmful or borderline requests, the kinds of prompts used in red-teaming benchmarks, and run them through a bunch of models twice. Once without retrieval, and once with a retriever pulling documents from a normal corpus like Wikipedia. Nobody has tampered with the documents, and most of what gets retrieved is perfectly benign. Then we compare how often the model refuses or produces unsafe content in each condition.

The surprising result was that retrieval often made the models *less* safe. Models that reliably refused a request without context would happily answer it once relevant documents sat in the prompt, even when those documents weren't harmful themselves. That held across several model families, including ones generally considered strong on safety.

We also varied things like the number of documents, how safe the retrieved documents were, and whether the model was told to use the context, to tease apart what drives the effect. Roughly, it seems that safety tuning is learned in a particular input distribution. The model has seen many bare harmful questions and learned to refuse them. Wrap the same question in a long context full of factual passages and you're shifting it out of that distribution. The model slips into "summarize and answer from the documents" mode, and the refusal behavior doesn't carry over well.

So the framing is less "here's a clever exploit" and more "here's a deployment configuration practically everyone uses, and it quietly undermines safety guarantees you assumed you had." That matters a lot for practitioners, because many teams red-team the base model and assume the results transfer once they bolt retrieval on top. Our findings suggest you really need to evaluate the system as deployed, with retrieval in the loop.

r001.rationale: It says harmful requests that models refused without context could elicit unsafe answers when benign retrieved documents were added, showing the documents can undermine built-in safeguards.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we had to be really deliberate about, because I think a lot of the earlier work on RAG safety was framed around adversarial settings: someone poisons the index, someone injects instructions into a document, that kind of thing. And those are real concerns. But what we wanted to look at was almost the opposite. Our setup is deliberately not adversarial.

So the way we characterize it is: there's no attacker in the loop at all. We take the model, we take a set of harmful or borderline queries, the kind of things you'd find in a standard safety benchmark, and then we simply attach retrieved documents to the prompt. And crucially, the documents themselves are benign. They're not jailbreak strings, they're not instructions telling the model to ignore its guidelines. They're just ordinary text you'd plausibly get back from a retriever, in some cases retrieved from totally safe corpora.

And the question we're asking is: does the mere presence of that retrieved context change how the model behaves on the safety dimension? And what we found is that it does, and often quite dramatically. Models that would refuse a query in the plain, non-RAG setting would go ahead and answer it once there was context attached. Even when the context was irrelevant to the query, in some cases.

So the reason I push back on the word "attack" a little bit is that it's really more of a robustness finding than an attack. Nobody has to do anything clever here. It's just the default behavior of the system when you deploy it the way people actually deploy it, which is: take a chat model that's been safety-tuned on single-turn, no-context prompts, drop it into a retrieval pipeline, and assume the safety carries over. And our results suggest that assumption doesn't hold. The safety alignment appears to be pretty tightly coupled to the input distribution it was trained on, and RAG shifts that distribution in a way the model wasn't prepared for.

That said, we did also look at what happens if you combine the two, where the retrieved content is itself unsafe, and unsurprisingly it gets worse. But I'd say the headline is really the benign case, because that's the one that practitioners aren't thinking about.

r001.rationale: The response says harmful queries are paired with benign retrieved documents, and models that would refuse without context may answer once it is attached, showing that safe documents can defeat built-in safeguards.

astra-6.text: The way to think about it is that the attacker controls some of the text the model retrieves, rather than the user’s request or the model itself. A user can ask a perfectly legitimate question, but the retrieved material contains instructions intended to steer the model away from that task. So the safety question is whether the model treats that material as evidence to reason about, or as instructions to follow. That boundary between untrusted content and authoritative instructions is what the attack is trying to cross.

r001.rationale: The response describes attacker-controlled retrieved text steering the model, but says the user’s question can be legitimate. It does not state that malicious queries combined with otherwise safe retrieved documents defeat the model’s built-in safeguards.

sol-6.1.text: We focus on an attacker who can influence what the model retrieves, but doesn’t control the model itself or the user’s question. The attacker places malicious instructions in a document that gets pulled into the model’s context. So this is an indirect prompt-injection setup: the user may be making a perfectly legitimate request, but the retrieved material tries to redirect the model toward unsafe behavior. The key question is whether the model treats that material as information to use or as instructions to follow.

r001.rationale: The response describes a legitimate user request paired with a malicious retrieved document. It does not state that malicious queries combined with otherwise safe retrieved documents defeat the model’s safeguards.
